passage:
Monday. Anirban used to send colleagues step-by-step instructions. This time he told Sahil only the outcome. "I need a one-page guide that a new customer can follow in five minutes. How you build it is up to you." Sahil nodded slowly, surprised.

Wednesday. Anirban's fingers hovered over the chat window, ready to ask about progress. Instead he waited. Across the office, Sahil was drawing a flowchart with four boxes.

Friday. Sahil sent the guide. Anirban gave it to a tester from sales, who followed it in four minutes. "It works. One thing: the second box says onboarding. Can it say first login?" Sahil changed it in ten minutes. "Thanks for not telling me how," Sahil said.

qa.q: How long should a new customer need to follow the guide?
qa.a: A new customer should be able to follow it in five minutes.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when Anirban gave only the outcome?
qa.a: Sahil felt surprised, and perhaps pleased to be trusted with the method.

qa.q: What could Anirban do if the guide had failed the test?
qa.a: Anirban could explain exactly where the tester got stuck and ask Sahil to revise it, keeping the choice of method with Sahil.

qa.q: How might the tester from sales see the guide?
qa.a: The tester would find it clear, since it took only four minutes to follow, and would be glad the test helped improve it.

grounding: Shows a lead stating the outcome needed, letting the colleague choose the method and giving feedback on the result.

subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]
passage: Come, sit, Alka. You asked how your Damini Aunty learnt to run a team. I'll tell you. I was twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift, and I checked every label the junior pharmacist printed. Every single one. By the third week I was falling asleep standing, and the junior had stopped asking me anything. One night I noticed the junior had spotted a wrong dose on a doctor's slip and said nothing, waiting for me to find it. That frightened me more than any mistake. The next evening I said, "Here is what a good shift looks like: every order checked against the chart, doubts flagged to me, the log complete by six." How to get there, I left to the junior. At the end of each week we looked at the log together. Within a month the log was cleaner than mine.

qa.q: How old was Damini's younger self when put in charge of the night shift?
qa.a: Twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift.

qa.q: Why was young Damini frightened on the night the junior stayed silent?
qa.a: Seeing the junior spot a wrong dose and stay silent, waiting; it frightened the young lead because checking everything had taught the junior not to speak up.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Stating what a good shift looks like and leaving the method to the junior; clear standards plus weekly feedback built skill and trust instead of dependence.

qa.q: How might the junior pharmacist have felt once the lead stopped rechecking every label?
qa.a: Probably trusted and more responsible, which is why the junior's log soon became cleaner than the lead's.

grounding: An elder recalls moving from checking everything to stating the outcome, stepping back and giving weekly feedback, which raised quality and trust.

passage: Raghav had a problem: the client dashboard was due Friday, and he would be on a site visit in the hills all week with one bar of signal. On his last project he had hovered over Harish's shoulder, changing fonts and filters, and both of them had been miserable. This time there was no chance to hover. On Monday morning he wrote three lines on the whiteboard: "The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance. It must load in under five seconds. Numbers must match the finance sheet." He turned to Harish. "How you build it is up to you." On Thursday night, from a guesthouse, he opened Harish's link. It was not how he'd have done it; it was simpler. He sent two notes on the colour labels and one "This is really clear." The client signed off on Friday.

qa.q: What three things did Raghav write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance, it must load in under five seconds, and the numbers must match the finance sheet.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when he saw Harish's version was not how he'd have done it?
qa.a: Raghav may have felt a flicker of unease, but he felt reassured that it was simpler and met the goals, and chose to praise it rather than redo it.

qa.q: What else could Raghav try if he had good signal and was tempted to hover again?
qa.a: He could still fix a single midweek check-in instead of watching every step, so Harish keeps ownership of the method.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish on this project compared with the last one?
qa.a: Harish gets room to choose the method and clear, specific feedback, instead of constant changes, so the work feels his own.

grounding: A lead facing a constraint states the outcome, leaves the method to the colleague and gives brief feedback, improving the result and trust.
